query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray gun traverse speed during APS deposition will increase the effective material deposition (by increasing splat overlap and dwell time) so that the FeCoNiCrAl bond coat reaches the required thickness while maintaining coating integrity and producing minimal additional in‐flight oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat produced using 15–45 μm feedstock under standard APS conditions, which yields a coating thinner than required.
generation.intervention: Lower the traverse speed (i.e. slow down the gun movement) during the thermal-spray process.
generation.conditions: Keep the plasma power, gas flows, stand-off distance, and ambient conditions constant; apply this modification during APS processing of the bond coat intended for use in a thermal barrier coating system at high service temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Longer particle residence time on the substrate enhances splat overlap and layer buildup without changing the melt or oxidation dynamics significantly.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the traverse speed, each substrate area is exposed longer to the spray, which allows more molten particles to accumulate and fuse. This greater overlap and thicker deposit is achieved without altering the thermal or reactive gas environment, thus preserving the intended phase integrity and keeping as-sprayed oxidation minimal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating will achieve a significantly increased thickness compared to the standard process (baseline 15–45 μm feedstock deposition) while retaining a dense, well-adherent microstructure with minimal oxide formation.
generation.baseline: Depositions using the typical, higher traverse speed yield bond coats that fall short of the required thickness.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if other APS parameters (e.g., plasma temperature, gas composition, stand-off distance) remain optimized; overly slow traverse speeds may risk overheating or localized oxidation increases.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal reduction in traverse speed and its absolute effect on both thickness and oxidation levels are not precisely known in advance and will need tuning to balance increased deposition with thermal exposure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of APS depositions of the FeCoNiCrAl alloy on standard substrates using identical plasma power, gas flow, and stand-off distance settings while varying only the traverse speed (e.g., standard speed vs. progressively lower speeds). Evaluate the resulting coating thickness, microstructural integrity, and oxidation content.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM imaging to obtain coating thickness
EDS or XRD analysis to assess oxidation levels
Adhesion and microstructural examinations to check coating integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the traverse speed does not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness relative to the baseline—or if the resulting deposits show enhanced oxidation or compromised microstructure (e.g., increased porosity or cracking)—then the hypothesis is falsified.

Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. cited_evidence.text: In this study, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit the coating by atmospheric plasma spraying. Prior to spraying, the feedstock powder was dried in an oven at 200 °C for 3 h to remove the moisture and improve its flowability. First, 316 stainless steel cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ 25 × 7 mm were used as substrates. Before spraying, the substrates were cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaner in acetone for 10 min, and then dried with a dryer. To improve the bonding strength of the coating, sand blasting one side of the substrate was carried out to obtain a certain cleanliness and roughness. During sand blasting, an Al2O3 particle with a size of less than 1.25 mm was used as an abrasive. The substrates were sandblasted under a compressed air pressure of about 0.5 MPa for 30 s. An APS system (3710, PRAXAIR SURFACE TECHNOLOGIES, Indianapolis, IN, USA) with a high-energy plasma gun (SG-100) was employed to deposit the coating. During spraying, argon was used as a primary gas, and nitrogen was used as a secondary gas, whose pressures were 0.4 and 0.3 MPa, respectively.
